Mary Berry Creamy Potatoes au Gratin

Mary Berry Creamy Potatoes au Gratin is the kind of side dish that turns a simple roast into a full-on event. Thin slices of waxy potato, ribbons of onion, and a blanket of melted Gruyère come together under a golden, bubbling crust. The result is equal parts tender and crisp — milky soft layers below, a deeply bronzed top above.

Total time clocks in at 75 minutes, and I would call this a beginner-friendly recipe with one small caveat: getting the potato slices uniformly thin matters more than you might think. It is the sort of dish you pull out for a Sunday roast, a holiday spread, or any cold-weather meal where comfort food earns its place at the table.

What is Mary Berry Creamy Potatoes au Gratin?

This is a classic French-inspired potato bake — thinly sliced waxy potatoes layered with onion, heavy cream, and grated cheese, then baked until the top crackles and the inside turns lush and tender. The method is straightforward: layer, cover, bake, uncover, and let the heat do the rest. What you get is a creamy, savory interior with a crisp cheese crust that shatters under a spoon. It sits somewhere between a dauphinoise and a scalloped potato dish, with enough richness to anchor a meal.

Why This Recipe is Worth Trying

A handful of reasons make this gratin a repeat contender in my kitchen.

  • Layered richness — every forkful delivers cream, melted cheese, and soft potato in one bite.
  • Golden, crackling crust — the butter-dotted top browns into something genuinely irresistible.
  • Straightforward technique — a mandoline or sharp knife and a single baking dish handle most of the work.
  • Holiday-worthy presence — it looks impressive on a buffet but requires no fancy skills.
  • Resting bonus — a 10-minute wait after baking sets the layers, making portioning clean and neat.

Essential Ingredients to Make Mary Berry Creamy Potatoes au Gratin

You probably have most of these already, but a couple of choices make a real difference in the final dish.

The Foundation

  • Waxy potatoes — 1 1/2 pounds (about 4 medium) such as Yukon Gold or Maris Piper, peeled and sliced into 1/8-inch-thick rounds. Waxy varieties hold their shape during baking instead of turning to mush.
  • Onion — 1 small one, thinly sliced to roughly 1/2 cup. It softens into near-invisibility while adding a gentle savory backbone.

The Creamy Elements

  • Heavy cream — 1 1/4 cups, also called double cream. This is the non-negotiable heart of the dish; half-and-half will not set up the same way.
  • Unsalted butter — 2 tablespoons softened, plus extra for greasing the dish. The butter dots on top are what drive that deep browning.

The Flavor Team

  • Garlic — 1 clove, halved and rubbed inside the dish, then discarded. It leaves a whisper of flavor without overpowering the cream.
  • Gruyère or sharp cheddar — 1 cup (4 ounces) grated. Gruyère melts into a nutty, smooth layer; sharp cheddar brings a punchier tang.
  • Kosher salt — 1 teaspoon. Draws moisture from the potatoes and seasons every layer evenly.
  • Black pepper — 1/4 teaspoon freshly ground. Pre-ground lacks the aromatic kick this dish deserves.
  • Freshly grated nutmeg — 1/4 teaspoon. Just enough to warm the cream without announcing itself.

Handy Kitchen Tools for Best Results

A few tools make the process smoother, though nothing here is particularly obscure.

  • Mandoline slicer — for uniform 1/8-inch rounds that cook evenly. A sharp knife works too, but consistency takes practice.
  • 1-quart gratin dish — shallow and wide promotes better browning than a deep casserole. Any similar-sized baking dish can substitute.
  • Large mixing bowl — gives you room to toss the potatoes and onion with cream without spills.
  • Aluminum foil — traps steam during the first bake, tenderizing the potatoes before the crust forms.
  • Sharp paring knife — the simplest test for doneness; it should slide through the center with zero resistance.

Step-by-Step Guide to Making Mary Berry Creamy Potatoes au Gratin

Seven steps, one dish, and a kitchen that smells incredible by the halfway mark.

  • Preheat and prep the dish — set the oven to 375°F (190°C). Grease a 1-quart gratin dish with butter, then rub the cut sides of the halved garlic clove over the bottom and sides. Discard the clove afterward.
  • Coat the potatoes and onion — in a large bowl, combine the sliced potatoes and onion. Pour the cream over them, add the salt, pepper, and nutmeg, then toss gently until every slice wears an even coating of seasoned cream.
  • Build the first layer — arrange one third of the potato-onion mixture in the dish, overlapping the slices slightly. Sprinkle one third of the grated cheese across the top.
  • Repeat the layers — add two more identical layers, finishing with the last of the cheese on top. Resist the urge to press down; the cream needs room to bubble through.
  • Dot with butter — distribute the 2 tablespoons of softened butter in small pieces across the surface. These bits melt into the cheese and drive the browning process.
  • Cover and bake — seal the dish tightly with aluminum foil and bake for 30 minutes. The trapped steam softens the potatoes without scorching the top.
  • Uncover and finish — remove the foil and bake another 20 to 25 minutes. Look for a deeply golden, bubbling top and test with a knife — it should meet no resistance in the center. Let the gratin rest 10 minutes before serving so the cream sets and the layers hold together.

What I Got Wrong (And How I Fixed It)

Here is what tripped me up the first few times and how to sidestep the same issues.

  • Slices cut too thick — potatoes over 1/8 inch stayed firm in the center while the edges overbrowned. A mandoline solved this instantly.
  • Skipping the foil step — going straight to an uncovered bake left the top burnt and the middle raw. That 30-minute covered steam is essential.
  • Using the wrong potato variety — starchy russets broke down into a grainy mash. Waxy potatoes like Yukon Gold kept their structure beautifully.
  • Rushing the rest time — slicing in too early released a puddle of hot cream onto the plate. Ten minutes of patience made clean, tidy portions.
  • Overloading the dish — cramming everything into too small a vessel prevented even cooking. A shallow 1-quart dish gave the cream space to reduce properly.
  • Grating nutmeg from a jar — pre-ground nutmeg tasted dull and slightly dusty. Freshly grated brought warmth that lifted the entire dish.

Healthier Version of Mary Berry Creamy Potatoes au Gratin

A few swaps can lighten this dish without stripping away its character.

  • Swap heavy cream for half-and-half — the sauce will be thinner but still creamy. Expect a less luxurious texture and compensate with an extra sprinkle of cheese.
  • Reduce the cheese by one third — cutting back to roughly 2/3 cup still gives you a respectable crust while trimming saturated fat.
  • Use a light butter alternative — a quality olive oil-based spread on top browns nearly as well as butter with fewer calories.
  • Add a layer of thinly sliced zucchini — swapping out one third of the potatoes for zucchini cuts carbohydrates and adds a subtle vegetal note.
  • Skip the butter dots on top — the crust will be less bronzed but still pleasant, and you save roughly 200 calories across the dish.

Ingredient Substitutions for Mary Berry Creamy Potatoes au Gratin

Not every pantry matches the original list, and these swaps hold up well.

  • 1 1/4 cups heavy cream → 1 cup whole milk + 1/4 cup melted butter — this blend mimics the fat content closely. The finished texture runs a touch looser but still satisfies.
  • 1 cup Gruyère → 1 cup Emmental or Comté — both melt into that same nutty, smooth layer. Emmental is milder; Comté brings more depth.
  • 1 cup sharp cheddar → 1 cup Red Leicester or Double Gloucester — these British cheeses deliver a similar tang and melt cleanly into the cream.
  • 1 1/2 pounds Yukon Gold → 1 1/2 pounds red-skinned new potatoes — another waxy option that holds its shape. The skin can stay on for a more rustic look if scrubbed well.
  • 1/4 teaspoon freshly grated nutmeg → 1/4 teaspoon ground mace — mace offers a comparable warmth with a slightly more floral edge. Use the same amount.
  • 1 small onion → 1 medium shallot, finely sliced — shallots bring a sweeter, more delicate flavor that melts into the background even more gracefully.

Pairing Ideas: What to Serve With Mary Berry Creamy Potatoes au Gratin

This gratin plays well with others — here are some combinations that make sense on the plate.

  • Simple roast chicken — the clean, herby flavor of a roast bird balances the richness of the gratin without competing.
  • Pan-seared steak with peppercorn sauce — the creamy potatoes soak up any extra sauce, and the crisp crust contrasts with tender beef.
  • Glazed carrots with thyme — a touch of sweetness and a pop of color cut through all that cream and cheese.
  • A sharply dressed green salad — lemon vinaigrette and bitter greens like arugula provide the acid this dish craves.
  • Poached white fish with dill — something light and flaky keeps the meal from tipping into heavy territory.
  • Steamed green beans with toasted almonds — crunch and freshness give the plate balance without adding another sauce.

Expert Tips to Make Perfect Mary Berry Creamy Potatoes au Gratin

Small details separate a good gratin from a great one.

  • Dry the potato slices thoroughly — patting them with a clean towel after slicing removes excess starch and helps the cream cling instead of turning watery.
  • Warm the cream slightly before tossing — room-temperature cream blends more evenly and shaves a few minutes off the baking time.
  • Overlap slices the same way in every layer — consistent layering means consistent cooking; no rogue slices poking up to burn.
  • Test doneness in three spots — the center and two edges should all yield to a knife with no resistance. One tender spot is not enough.
  • Broil for the final 2 minutes if needed — if the top is not quite golden after the uncovered bake, a quick blast under the broiler finishes it without overcooking the interior.
  • Season each layer lightly as you build — a tiny pinch of salt and pepper between layers guarantees flavor all the way through, not just on top.
  • Use the butter wrapper to grease the dish — an old trick that wastes nothing and coats the dish evenly before the garlic rub.

Creative Ways to Customize Mary Berry Creamy Potatoes au Gratin

Once you have the base method down, these variations keep the dish feeling new.

  • Add crispy bacon lardons — scatter cooked, crispy bacon between the layers for a smoky, salty crunch that plays off the cream beautifully.
  • Tuck in fresh thyme or rosemary — a few sprigs nestled into the layers infuse the cream with herbal notes as it bakes.
  • Swap in blue cheese — replace half the Gruyère with crumbled Stilton or Roquefort for a bold, tangy twist that pairs well with steak.
  • Introduce a mustard kick — stir a teaspoon of Dijon mustard into the cream before tossing. It adds warmth and a subtle sharpness.
  • Grate Parmesan over the top layer — a dusting of finely grated Parmesan in the last 10 minutes of baking creates an extra-crisp, savory crust.
  • Fold in sautéed leeks — softened leeks layered in with the potatoes bring a sweeter, more rounded allium flavor than onion alone.

Storing Mary Berry Creamy Potatoes au Gratin the Right Way

Leftovers keep well if you treat them properly.

  • Refrigerate in an airtight container — transfer cooled portions to a sealed container and store for up to 3 days. The flavors actually deepen overnight.
  • Cover the baking dish directly — if you plan to reheat the whole thing, press plastic wrap directly onto the surface, then add foil. This prevents a skin from forming.
  • Freeze for up to one month — wrap the cooled, baked gratin tightly in a double layer of foil and freeze. The texture may turn slightly grainy upon reheating, but the flavor remains solid.
  • Thaw overnight in the refrigerator — never reheat from frozen; slow thawing gives the cream a chance to reabsorb into the potatoes.
  • Portion before freezing for quick meals — cutting the gratin into individual squares and freezing them separately makes weekday reheating far easier.

How to Reheat Mary Berry Creamy Potatoes au Gratin (If Needed)

Reheating gently keeps the cream from separating and the potatoes from drying out.

  • Oven method at 350°F (175°C) — place the gratin in an oven-safe dish, cover loosely with foil, and warm for 15 to 20 minutes. Remove the foil for the last 5 minutes to re-crisp the top.
  • Microwave option for speed — use a microwave-safe plate, cover with a damp paper towel, and heat in 30-second bursts. The crust will soften, but the interior stays creamy.
  • Air fryer revival — set to 320°F (160°C) and heat for 5 to 7 minutes. The circulating air does wonders for bringing back some crispness to the top.
  • Stovetop in a covered skillet — add a splash of cream or milk to a nonstick pan, place the portion in, cover, and warm over low heat for 8 to 10 minutes. Steam does the work without scorching.

FAQs

Can I prepare Mary Berry Creamy Potatoes au Gratin ahead of time?

Yes. Assemble the entire dish up to the point of baking, cover it tightly, and refrigerate for up to 24 hours. When ready, bake straight from the fridge, adding roughly 10 extra minutes to the covered baking time.

What is the best potato for this gratin?

Waxy varieties like Yukon Gold or Maris Piper work best because they keep their shape during the long bake. Avoid floury potatoes such as russets, which tend to break down and turn the dish grainy.

Why did my gratin turn out watery?

Excess moisture usually comes from not drying the potato slices or using a potato variety that releases too much starch. Patting the slices dry and sticking with waxy potatoes fixes this almost every time.

How long does Mary Berry Creamy Potatoes au Gratin last in the fridge?

Stored properly in an airtight container, it keeps for up to 3 days. The cream sets further as it cools, which actually makes reheated portions slice more cleanly.

Can I freeze Mary Berry Creamy Potatoes au Gratin?

You can freeze the baked and cooled gratin for up to one month. Be aware that the texture may turn slightly grainy after thawing due to the cream separating, though the flavor stays intact.

Do I have to peel the potatoes?

Peeling is recommended for the smoothest texture, since skins can curl and create uneven layers. That said, thin-skinned waxy potatoes like Yukon Gold work fine unpeeled if you scrub them well and slice them very thin.

Wrapping It Up

Mary Berry Creamy Potatoes au Gratin is one of those rare dishes that feels both effortless and indulgent. Give it a spot on your next dinner table — the empty dish at the end speaks louder than anything I could write here.

Mary Berry Creamy Potatoes au Gratin

Print Recipe
Print Recipe

Thinly sliced potatoes layered with rich cream, savory onion, and melted cheese, baked until golden and bubbling. A luxurious side dish with a tender, milky interior and a crisp, cheesy crust.

  • Author: Ekani Ella
  • Prep Time: 20
  • Cook Time: 55
  • Total Time: 75
  • Yield: 4 1x
  • Category: Side Dish
  • Method: Baking
  • Cuisine: French, British

Ingredients

Scale
  • 2 tablespoons unsalted butter, softened, plus extra for greasing the dish
  • 1 garlic clove, halved
  • 1 1/2 pounds (about 4 medium) waxy potatoes such as Yukon Gold or Maris Piper, peeled and sliced into 1/8-inch-thick rounds
  • 1 small onion, thinly sliced (about 1/2 cup)
  • 1 1/4 cups heavy cream (double cream)
  • 1 cup (4 ounces) grated Gruyère or sharp cheddar cheese
  • 1 teaspoon kosher salt
  • 1/4 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper
  • 1/4 teaspoon freshly grated nutmeg

Instructions

  1. Preheat the oven to 375°F (190°C). Grease a 1-quart gratin dish or shallow baking dish with butter. Rub the cut sides of the garlic clove all over the bottom and sides of the dish to impart a subtle garlic flavor, then discard the clove.
  2. In a large bowl, combine the sliced potatoes and onion. Pour the cream over the mixture, add salt, pepper, and nutmeg, and toss gently until every slice is evenly coated with the seasoned cream.
  3. Arrange one third of the potato and onion mixture in the prepared dish, overlapping the slices slightly in an even layer. Sprinkle with one third of the grated cheese. Repeat layering twice more, finishing with the remaining cheese on top.
  4. Dot the top with the 2 tablespoons of softened butter, distributing small pieces evenly over the surface to promote browning and enrich the crust.
  5. Cover the dish tightly with aluminum foil. Bake for 30 minutes, allowing the potatoes to steam and become tender without the top burning.
  6. Remove the foil and continue baking for an additional 20 to 25 minutes, or until the top is deeply golden brown and bubbly, and a knife inserted into the center meets no resistance from the potatoes.
  7. Let the gratin rest for 10 minutes before serving. This resting time allows the cream to set slightly, making it easier to portion and ensuring the layers hold together.

Notes

Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat in a 350°F (175°C) oven for 15-20 minutes until hot. To freeze, wrap the baked and cooled gratin tightly; freeze for up to 1 month. Thaw overnight in the refrigerator and reheat, though the texture may become slightly grainy.
